questions.label: Intent
questions.text: In plain English, what is this exercise for, and what happens in it? (exercise control only)
questions.why: It is the yardstick every later answer is checked against.

questions.label: Unit
questions.text: Which team or unit trains, and what is its job?
questions.why: Every task, condition and standard is written for this team.

questions.label: Team Size and Positions
questions.text: How many people train, and in which positions?
questions.why: It decides how many tasks can run at once and whom the controllers watch.

questions.label: Proficiency
questions.text: How experienced are the team with this kind of situation?
questions.why: It sets how hard the scenario can push and how much help the controllers give.

questions.label: Mandate
questions.text: What are the team responsible for protecting or achieving, and which actions are open to them?
questions.why: It defines what counts as a good decision in play.

questions.label: Time Slot
questions.text: How long does the exercise run, and when?
questions.why: The tasks, the events and the review all have to fit inside it.
questions.recommended: Four hours, then a one-hour review

questions.label: Setting
questions.text: Where does the exercise run?
questions.why: It decides what has to be built or booked before the day.
options: In a lab or on real equipment
Distributed, each person at their own station

questions.label: Real or Fictional World
questions.text: Does it use real country and organization names, or a fictional world?
questions.why: A fictional world avoids real-world sensitivities and lets the team speak freely.

questions.label: Handling and Recording
questions.text: How is the exercise handled and recorded: classification, notes, screen capture, AI tools?
questions.why: It sets what the team can write down and what leaves the room.

questions.label: Collective Tasks
questions.text: Which collective tasks does the team train? One per item.
questions.why: The exercise exists to train these; everything else serves them.

questions.label: Standards
questions.text: What standard must the team meet on each task? One per item, in the same order as the tasks.
questions.why: A task without a standard can't be evaluated.

questions.label: Conditions
questions.text: Under what conditions does the team work: time pressure, degraded systems, missing people?
questions.why: Conditions make the same task easier or harder; they are what controllers vary.

questions.label: Evaluation Method
questions.text: How is each task evaluated?
questions.why: Trained, practiced or untrained gives the commander a reading per task, not just a pass or a fail.

questions.label: Kind of Training
questions.text: What kind of training is this?
questions.why: It sets how the exercise is evaluated and reported.

questions.label: Rules of Engagement
questions.text: What may the team do, and not do, during play?
questions.why: It keeps play realistic and stops the exercise turning into something it isn't.

questions.label: Deadline
questions.text: Is there a point by which the team must act, and what happens if they miss it?
questions.why: A fixed point forces the decision the exercise is built around.

questions.label: Pacing
questions.text: How does time run in the exercise?
questions.why: It decides how injects are timed and how long each decision can take.

questions.label: Adjudication
questions.text: Who decides the outcome of what participants do?
questions.why: Someone has to rule on what each action achieves, and everyone should know who.

questions.label: Teaching Points
questions.text: What should the team take away even if the exercise goes wrong? One per item (controllers only).
questions.why: They steer the review when the tasks don't go to plan.

questions.label: One-Line Problem
questions.text: In one line, what does the team face when the exercise starts?
questions.why: The team hears this first, so it has to be clear and short.

questions.label: Participant Description
questions.text: In one paragraph a participant could read, what is the scenario about?
questions.why: Catalogs, invitations and read-ins all start from it. It must not give the twist away.

questions.label: Place and Time
questions.text: Where and when is the scenario set: region, era, time of year?
questions.why: Places and dates stay consistent across every inject and document.

questions.label: Ground Truth
questions.text: List what is really happening, one fact per item (controllers only).
questions.why: Only the controllers know the ground truth. Later checks use these facts to catch leaks.

questions.label: Opposition
questions.text: Who or what works against the team?
questions.why: It decides how many controllers you need and how unpredictable the exercise is.

questions.label: Adversary
questions.text: Who is the opposition, what does it want, and what is at stake for it? (exercise control only)
questions.why: The opposition plays to a goal, not at random.

questions.label: Threat Actor Capability
questions.text: How capable is the threat actor? (exercise control only)
questions.why: It bounds what the adversary can plausibly do in play.

questions.label: ATT&CK Techniques
questions.text: Which ATT&CK techniques does the adversary use? One per item, such as "T1566 Phishing" (exercise control only).
questions.why: Techniques tie the scenario to real behaviour, and to the injects and detections that test it.

questions.label: Systems in Play
questions.text: Which systems, networks or equipment does the team work on? One per item.
questions.why: Range builders and controllers prepare exactly these.

questions.label: Key Events
questions.text: What key events do the controllers push, in order? One per item: when, who delivers it, what happens, and the response you expect (controllers only).
questions.why: They make sure every task gets tested, whatever the team does.

questions.label: Branching
questions.text: How does the scenario change depending on what the team do? (exercise control only)
questions.why: Controllers need to know which way to steer before play starts.

questions.label: Escalation Ceiling
questions.text: How hard can it get before the controllers ease off?
questions.why: Past this point the team stops learning.

questions.label: Escalation Steps
questions.text: What are the escalation steps, in order? One per item; mark the last one the team can still recover from (exercise control only).
questions.why: Controllers can see how close play is to the ceiling.

questions.label: Ending
questions.text: How does the exercise end, and on what?
questions.why: The controllers need to know when to call it.

questions.label: Fog
questions.text: How much of the picture do participants see?
questions.why: What they are not shown, on purpose, is part of what the exercise tests.
questions.recommended: Partial: each role sees what it would
options: Partial: each role sees what it would
Full: only what is reported to them

questions.label: Range Reference
questions.text: Which range does it build on: the provider, the enclave, and the base image or network, if known?
questions.why: The network module starts from this instead of from nothing.
questions.recommended: GraySpace; enclave and base to be chosen with the range team

questions.label: Network Segments
questions.text: Which network segments or enclaves does the scenario need, and what is each for? One per item.
questions.why: The network module builds one segment for each.

questions.label: Hosts
questions.text: Which hosts sit on each segment: role, operating system, rough count? One per item, such as "OT network: historian, Windows Server 2019, 1".
questions.why: It sizes the build and decides which images are needed.

questions.label: Services
questions.text: Which services run on the range, and on which hosts? One per item, such as "Email: mail01".
questions.why: Services decide what the team defends and what the scenario's attacker uses.

questions.label: Connectivity
questions.text: What talks to what, and what reaches the internet?
questions.why: Routes and firewall rules decide which attack paths exist.

questions.label: Identity and Accounts
questions.text: How are identities set up: domain, user accounts, service accounts?
questions.why: Accounts are often how the scenario's attacker gets in, and how the team traces them.

questions.label: Defenses and Sensors
questions.text: What defends the network, and what can the team see with: firewalls, EDR, SIEM, packet capture, logs? One per item.
questions.why: The team can only find what its sensors record.

questions.label: Telemetry
questions.text: What is recorded for the review? One per item: logs, network traffic, endpoint activity, chat.
questions.why: The review can only show what was recorded.

questions.label: Platforms
questions.text: Which websites, email, chat or social media must exist on the range? One per item.
questions.why: Simulated users need somewhere to work, and information injects need somewhere to appear.

questions.label: Simulated Users
questions.text: Which simulated users should be on the network (NPCs): how many, in which roles, doing what? (controllers only)
questions.why: Background activity hides the attack the way real users would.

questions.label: Planted Before Start
questions.text: What must be in place before the exercise starts: vulnerabilities, malware, files, log history? One per item (controllers only).
questions.why: The key events only work if these are there on the day.

questions.label: Build Limits
questions.text: What limits the build: scale, images that must be used, air-gapped, time to build?
questions.why: The network module has to fit inside these.

gate.approval: Approve the control plan and names

questions.label: Control Cell
questions.text: Who controls, who observes and evaluates, and who plays the opposition?
questions.why: Each role needs a named person before the exercise starts.

questions.label: Safety and Stop
questions.text: What stops the exercise for a real-world problem, and who can call it?
questions.why: Everyone must know how to stop, and how play restarts.
questions.recommended: Anyone can say "real world, stop"; the lead controller restarts it

questions.label: Exercise Name
questions.text: What is the exercise's name?
questions.why: Short and easy to say over a radio or a call, and not reused from an earlier exercise.

questions.label: Organizations
questions.text: Which organizations appear in the scenario, and whose side is each on: friendly, adversary or neutral? One per item, such as "Harrow Port Authority: friendly".
questions.why: Names stay the same in every event and document.

questions.label: Fixed Terms
questions.text: Which terms must everyone use the same way? One per item.
questions.why: Shared terms keep reports and events consistent.

questions.label: Banned Terms
questions.text: Which words must the scenario avoid? One per item.
questions.why: Some words give the twist away or touch real-world sensitivities.
